summary: Ahtahkakoop’s treaty-era history is closely connected to Sandy Lake and the Green Lake Trail. Chief Ahtahkakoop signed Treaty 6 at Fort Carlton on August 23, 1876, seeking reserve land beside Mistawasis where his people already maintained homes and gardens. The 1878 survey did not provide the location or area requested. Agriculture became an important part of reserve life, but falling crop prices in 1929 and subsequent drought pushed some members to seek work elsewhere. These events describe one period of the community’s history, rather than the beginning of its people’s relationship with the land.
detail: Basil Starblanket succeeded Ahtahkakoop after his death in 1896. The Nation’s publishing company issued a substantial history of Ahtahkakoop and his people in 2000.
connections: The encyclopedia records Ahtahkakoop’s request for reserve land adjoining Mistawasis along the Green Lake Trail.

summary: Beardy’s and Okemasis’ Cree Nation’s history includes hunting and trapping around Duck Lake before Treaty 6. Chief Beardy, also known as Kahmeeyistoowaysit, signed at Fort Carlton on August 28, 1876. He selected land west of Duck Lake for his people and those of Chief Okemasis, or Sayswaypus. Members built log homes and cultivated gardens there. A monument erected in 1953 commemorated lives lost during the 1885 Resistance. In 1991, the Nation and Saskatchewan Provincial Parks agreed to establish a tipi encampment at Fort Carlton, connecting the historic site with the community’s own interpretation of its past.
detail: Community justice initiatives later included sentencing and healing circles involving Elders. The Willow Cree Healing Lodge opened in 2003.

summary: Big River Cree First Nation’s history is rooted in the forests, lakes and waterways northwest of Prince Albert. Chief See-See-Way-um signed Treaty 6 on September 3, 1878. The encyclopedia describes the following two decades as a period when members supported themselves through hunting, trapping and fishing. Kenemotayoo succeeded him as chief, and a district trail carried his name. The area’s history also includes the Carlton Trail, an important fur-trade route between Edmonton and Winnipeg. These treaty and trade records describe particular historical encounters; they do not establish when Indigenous people first lived along the Big River.

Black Lake Denesuline First Nation’s ancestors joined Treaty 8 at Fond du Lac in July 1899 under Chief Maurice Piche, also known as Moberley. The people continued hunting, fishing and trapping over a much wider territory, including areas now within the Northwest Territories. The encyclopedia dates the formal division of Piche’s band into Black Lake and Fond du Lac bands to 1949. Black Lake was also historically called the Stony Rapids Band. Its reserves lie around Black Lake in northern Saskatchewan. The administrative division and treaty adhesion are milestones in the written record, rather than the origin of Denesuline occupation of the region.
connections: Black Lake and Fond du Lac emerged from the formal division of Maurice Piche’s band, dated to 1949 in the encyclopedia.

summary: Buffalo River Dene Nation’s treaty history is connected to the former Peter Pond Band and Treaty 10, signed on August 28, 1906. The encyclopedia associates the people with Buffalo Narrows before settlement at Buffalo River, while treating the earlier movement as a historical interpretation. The Peter Pond Band divided into Buffalo River and Turnor Lake in 1972; Turnor Lake is now Birch Narrows Dene Nation. Hunting and trapping around Watapi Lake were important livelihoods. Establishment of the Primrose Lake Air Weapons Range in 1954 restricted harvesting and travel, contributing to later claims for losses of land access and economic opportunities.
connections: Buffalo River and Turnor Lake, now Birch Narrows, were formerly part of the Peter Pond Band and became separate bands in 1972.

summary: Carry the Kettle Nakoda Nation’s documented reserve history includes a major relocation from the Cypress Hills region. After joining Treaty 4 on September 25, 1877, the people sought reserve land west of the Cypress Hills. In June 1882 they were moved toward Indian Head, and their reserve south of Sintaluta was surveyed in 1885. Historical leaders included Long Lodge, Man Who Took the Coat and Carry the Kettle, who became chief in 1891. Agriculture, livestock, hay production, craft work and wage labour supported families through the reserve period. This account concerns treaty-era administration and relocation, within a much older Nakoda history.

facts.Historical leaders: Long Lodge; Man Who Took the Coat; Carry the Kettle

summary: Clearwater River Dene Nation’s history is tied to La Loche and the surrounding northern lakes. Historical accounts also use the names Big C and La Loche Band. Dene language and land-based work, especially fishing and trapping, are central features of the university’s account. The entry describes ancestors selecting the La Loche area for its vegetation and wildlife, and members living both on reserve and in La Loche itself. Its treaty reference differs from OpenBand’s existing source record, so an exact adhesion date is not repeated here. The community’s own history and the original treaty records require separate consideration when resolving that discrepancy.
detail: The encyclopedia associates ancestors with Treaty 8 in 1899, while OpenBand currently lists Treaty 10. This brief leaves the treaty field unresolved instead of treating either entry as conclusive.

summary: Cote First Nation’s treaty-era history includes Chief Gabriel Cote’s signing of Treaty 4 on September 15, 1874. His followers included Cree and Saulteaux people, and a reserve was surveyed in 1877. Subsequent land transactions around Kamsack repeatedly altered the reserve. Land was taken out of reserve status for a railway station and townsite in 1904, with further surrenders in the following years. Some land was later restored, including a southern strip returned in 1915 and additional acreage in 1963. This changing land base is an important part of the community’s historical experience and should be distinguished from its longer Indigenous history.

Cowessess First Nation’s treaty history includes Chief Cowessess, whose name is also recorded as Ka-wezauce, signing Treaty 4 on September 15, 1874. His followers included Saulteaux, Cree and Métis people. Families continued moving across their territory before some began farming near Maple Creek in 1878–79. A reserve was surveyed at Crooked Lake in 1880; while some members settled under O’Soup, Cowessess and others remained in the Cypress Hills until 1883. Education and mission institutions later shaped reserve life, including the opening of Cowessess Indian Residential School in 1898. These colonial-era milestones do not encompass the whole history of the community.

Cumberland House Cree Nation joined Treaty 5 through an adhesion in September 1876. Its reserve was surveyed in 1883, including Chief’s Island, where the chief, a councillor and other members lived. The chief sought additional land near Fort à la Corne because of its agricultural potential, but officials refused a reserve outside the treaty area. Members grew vegetables on Chief’s Island, while grain cultivation proved less successful. Hunting, fishing and trapping remained important to community life alongside later forestry and guiding work. The written account focuses on treaty and reserve decisions rather than defining the beginning of Cree presence in the region.

Day Star First Nation’s history includes hunting along the south branch of the Saskatchewan River before Chief Day Star, Kii-si-caw-ah-chuck, signed Treaty 4 on September 15, 1874. A reserve was surveyed in 1876, with later boundary changes. Early farming included a jointly maintained community garden and a practice of sharing cattle so other families could establish herds. The arrival of the railway at Lipton in 1905 created a market for produce. Agricultural work later changed with mechanization, including a tractor purchase in 1946. These details document adaptation during the reserve period without reducing the community’s older history to a treaty date.

Hatchet Lake Denesuline’s treaty adhesion followed negotiations at Lac du Brochet in August 1907. Commissioner Thomas Borthwick met the Lac la Hache people on August 19; after choosing their chief and headmen, they signed Treaty 10 on August 22. The people’s hunting, fishing and trapping extended beyond a permanent settlement. The encyclopedia describes a shift toward year-round community life as regular school attendance increased around 1960. Their reserve on the eastern side of Wollaston Lake was surveyed in 1965 and set apart in 1970. The earlier name Axe Lake helps explain the English name Hatchet Lake, alongside the French Lac la Hache.

Ministikwan Lake Cree Nation’s reserve history includes a long effort to obtain a separate land base. When the people entered Treaty 6 in 1876 without a chief recognized by officials, they were treated as part of Seekaskootch’s Onion Lake band. A 1907 petition sought their own reserve, leading to action in 1909 and establishment of the Island Lake Reserve in 1911. Officials did not follow the requested shoreline boundaries, which were intended to protect fish stocks. Hunting, fishing and trapping continued alongside gardening and forestry work. These administrative decisions describe reserve creation, rather than the beginning of the people’s connection to the lake.
connections: Officials initially grouped the Ministikwan people with Seekaskootch’s Onion Lake band; Ministikwan later petitioned for a separate reserve.

summary: James Smith Cree Nation’s written treaty history includes James Smith’s movement from St. Peter’s Reserve in Manitoba in 1875 and his signing of Treaty 6 on August 23, 1876. A reserve east of Prince Albert was surveyed in 1884. Later government actions brought people from other historical bands onto the reserve, including members of Chakastaypasin after its land was removed from reserve status in 1898 and Peter Chapman through an amalgamation in 1902. The encyclopedia discusses land grievances arising from these decisions. These historical band identities should be preserved in the account, rather than treating the community as having a single administrative origin.

Kahkewistahaw First Nation’s history includes Cree and Saulteaux people who hunted in the Wood Mountain and Cypress Hills regions. Chief Kahkewistahaw signed Treaty 4 on September 15, 1874. Families returned to the Qu’Appelle Valley for treaty payments before a reserve was surveyed in 1881. Agriculture developed despite difficult weather, but a large surrender in January 1907 removed much of the band’s most productive land and displaced farmers. A specific claim submitted in 1989 led to a settlement agreement signed on June 25, 2003. The claim and its resolution form part of the Nation’s continuing response to treaty-era land losses.

Kawacatoose First Nation’s treaty-era history includes Chief Kawacatoose signing Treaty 4 on September 15, 1874. Reserve land in the Big Touchwood Hills followed two years later. Colonial records often called the reserve Poor Man, although the encyclopedia translates Kawacatoose more closely as Lean Man or Skinny Man. After the chief’s death, his son Tawequasequape succeeded him. Members combined agriculture with sales of wood, hay and fence materials; a community farm began in 1949. In 1981, administration of the day school passed from Indian Affairs to the Nation. These events document changes in land, livelihoods and educational control during the reserve period.

Keeseekoose First Nation’s treaty history includes Chief Keeseekoose’s signing of Treaty 4 on September 15, 1874. The people initially settled on the Swan River Reserve in Manitoba, but flooding led to relocation to the Pelly and Kamsack area in Saskatchewan. Their reserve lies between Cote and The Key. The university account also records the later placement of the band-controlled St. Phillip’s School on the former residential-school grounds. The relocation is an important part of the Nation’s reserve history; neither it nor the treaty signing represents the beginning of the people’s Indigenous history.

Lac La Ronge Indian Band’s recorded history includes the James Roberts Wood Cree Band’s adhesion to Treaty 6 at Montreal Lake on February 11, 1889. Families hunted, fished and trapped around Lac la Ronge, maintaining lakeside camps and gardens. Communities developed at Lac la Ronge and Stanley Mission. Indian Affairs treated them as the James Roberts and Amos Charles bands in 1910, with separate annuity lists and funds but without formally dividing reserve land. The two bands were amalgamated on March 27, 1950. Their earlier land use and community identities extended beyond the boundaries and administrative names found in these records.
connections: Montreal Lake and Lac La Ronge shared the Little Red River agricultural reserve before its division in 1948.

summary: Little Black Bear First Nation’s history includes Cree and Assiniboine families who hunted and camped in the Cypress Hills during the nineteenth century. Chief Little Black Bear, recorded as Kees kee hew mus-coo muskwa, signed Treaty 4 on September 15, 1874. The band later settled on reserve land surveyed in the File Hills in 1880. Farming became an important part of reserve life, shaped by weather, available equipment and government policy. The treaty and reserve survey document changes in the community’s relationship with the Crown; they do not mark the beginning of its people or their connections to the Plains.

Little Pine First Nation’s ancestors were associated with the Cypress Hills before Chief Minahikosis, or Little Pine, joined Treaty 6 near Fort Walsh in 1879. The people were later moved to the Battle River area. Requests for adjoining reserves with Lucky Man, Poundmaker and Big Bear were refused. Little Pine died in 1885, and his people were dispersed during that period. A reserve for remaining Little Pine and Lucky Man members was surveyed in 1887. A treaty land entitlement settlement on May 29, 1997 addressed an inadequate land allocation and enabled further land purchases.
connections: Little Pine and Lucky Man members shared a reserve after dispersal in 1885; both sought adjoining reserves in the earlier treaty period.

summary: Lucky Man Cree Nation’s treaty-era history includes Papaway, or Lucky Man, who was a headman in Big Bear’s band when he adhered to Treaty 6 at Fort Walsh in 1879. The people moved toward Battleford in 1883. The following year, a request for a reserve adjoining Poundmaker, Little Pine and Big Bear was refused. Many Lucky Man and Little Pine members were dispersed in 1885; some settled together on Little Pine’s reserve. Research begun in 1972 supported a land claim that led to selection of land in the Thickwood Hills in 1989.
connections: Some Lucky Man members lived on Little Pine’s reserve following the dispersal of both communities in 1885.

summary: Makwa Sahgaiehcan First Nation’s history is connected to Makwa Lake and the Loon Lake district. The university account records the Makwa Lake Cree Band joining Treaty 6 on September 9, 1876. Members continued their established way of life for decades before obtaining the Makwa Lake reserves in 1916. Cattle raising and farming became important after the reserve land base was secured. This distinction matters: the 1916 reserve decision was an administrative milestone, rather than the origin of the Cree community. The historical name Loon Lake also appears in accounts of the band.

Mistawasis Nehiyawak’s treaty history includes Chief Mistawasis, leader of the Cree House People, signing Treaty 6 on August 23, 1876. A reserve was surveyed at Snake Plains in 1878, where wood, water, hay and agricultural land supported the community. The Green Lake Trail crossed the reserve and connected it with markets and freighting work. A school was established in 1878. The university account also records a 2001 settlement concerning land surrendered in 1911, 1917 and 1919. These treaty, transport and land-claim events form one part of a history rooted in Cree kinship and land use.
connections: Ahtahkakoop requested reserve land adjoining Mistawasis along the Green Lake Trail.

summary: Montreal Lake Cree Nation’s ancestors moved from the Grand Rapids region near Lake Winnipeg to Montreal Lake during the nineteenth century. Under Chief William Charles, the band joined Treaty 6 on February 11, 1889. A reserve was surveyed at the south end of Montreal Lake in 1890. The Little Red River Reserve was later surveyed for shared agricultural use with Lac La Ronge and divided in 1948. A Hudson’s Bay Company post established in 1891 became a regional freighting depot. Road and air transport later changed employment and helped develop tourism, alongside forestry and other activities.
connections: The two bands shared the Little Red River agricultural reserve before its division in 1948.

summary: Moosomin First Nation’s treaty record differs from the original Treaty 6 negotiations in 1876. Yellow Sky’s band was absent from those talks; his headman Moosomin signed an adhesion in spring 1881. A reserve near Battleford was surveyed that year, and Moosomin became chief in 1884. Railway construction through the reserve in 1903 increased employment and market access but was followed by pressure for its land. A surrender in 1909 led to relocation near Cochin. The Nation challenged the surrender in a claim submitted in 1986, and a settlement was ratified in 2003.

Mosquito, Grizzly Bear’s Head, Lean Man brings together historical bands with distinct treaty-era paths. Misketo signed a Treaty 6 adhesion on August 29, 1878, succeeding Little Chief; the Mosquito people settled in the Eagle Hills in 1879–80. Grizzly Bear’s Head had joined Treaty 4 under Tepee Hoska in 1877 before moving toward Battleford after his death. Lean Man also entered Treaty 4 and later settled in the Treaty 6 area. The encyclopedia records a merger in 1951. This history explains why a single modern treaty label cannot fully describe the component bands’ experiences.

Muscowpetung First Nation’s treaty history includes an Ojibway and Cree band joining Treaty 4 under Chief Muscowpetung on September 8, 1875. The people continued moving through the Cypress Hills region before settling on a reserve surveyed beside Pasqua in 1881. Agriculture developed after settlement. In 1882, the chief requested an extension westward along the Qu’Appelle River to gain better access to wood; officials changed other boundaries as part of that adjustment. These decisions illustrate how access to resources shaped the reserve’s development, alongside the people’s older relationships with the surrounding territory.
connections: Muscowpetung’s reserve was surveyed adjoining Pasqua’s reserve in 1881.

summary: Muskeg Lake Cree Nation joined Treaty 6 on August 23, 1876 under Chief Kitowehow, whose name also appears as Keetoowahan or Keetoowahaw. Members continued established livelihoods after treaty, selling furs and planting small potato plots. A reserve adjoining Mistawasis was surveyed in 1881. Its hay meadows, farmland, water and timber supported later farming and other work. The university account records employment with nearby settlers during the late 1880s and later commercial development. The treaty and survey belong to the reserve-era written record; they do not define the full extent of the Nation’s Cree history.
connections: Muskeg Lake’s original surveyed reserve adjoined Mistawasis on its southern boundary.

summary: Muskoday First Nation’s history includes ancestors from St. Peter’s Reserve near Selkirk, Manitoba. John Smith, Mis-ti-koo-na-pac, and his followers signed Treaty 6 at Fort Carlton on August 23, 1876. Their reserve southeast of Prince Albert was surveyed the following month. Many families settled in river lots, while later surveys divided other land into sections. Farming and cattle raising were important in the early reserve period, and a band farm was established in 1963. In 1998, Muskoday adopted its own land code, an important change in the administration of leasing and land development.

Muskowekwan First Nation’s ancestors lived around the Upper Qu’Appelle Lakes before joining Treaty 4 under Chief Ka-nee-na-wup on September 15, 1874. His son Muscowequan, also called Hard Quill, later became chief. A reserve surveyed in 1883 included an existing farming settlement near Touchwood Post. Agriculture and educational institutions shaped subsequent reserve life. The university account records ratification of a treaty land entitlement claim in 1993, enabling the Nation to expand its land holdings. These recorded changes concern treaty and reserve administration within a longer Ojibway history of the region.

Nekaneet Cree First Nation’s history is closely connected to remaining in the Cypress Hills when other communities were forced away in 1882. The university account associates the band’s Treaty 4 relationship with Foremost Man, also called Front Man, in 1874. Members were denied reserve land for decades before a small reserve near Maple Creek was established on August 2, 1913. Further land was added in 1958. Access to treaty benefits and schooling was also delayed. Later claims sought recognition of outstanding obligations. This history centres persistence in the people’s homeland, rather than treating reserve creation as the community’s beginning.

Ocean Man First Nation’s treaty-era history includes Chief Kitchi-Kah-Me-Win’s adhesion to Treaty 4 on September 9, 1875. A reserve beside Pheasant Rump in the Moose Mountains was surveyed in 1882. The people developed farms, but surrendered their reserve and were amalgamated with White Bear in 1901 after sustained pressure. Descendants later pursued a land claim and the restoration of their separate community. The band was re-established in 1988 and its reserve in 1992. The restored Nation carries an earlier history that continued through displacement; its modern administrative re-establishment was not the beginning of its people.
connections: Ocean Man was amalgamated with White Bear in 1901 before its separate band status was restored in 1988.
The original Ocean Man and Pheasant Rump reserves were adjacent in the Moose Mountains.

summary: Ochapowace First Nation’s written history includes the distinct Kakisheway and Chacachas bands. Kakisheway, also known as Loud Voice, signed Treaty 4 on September 15, 1874. His reserve was surveyed near Round Lake and the Qu’Appelle River in 1876. Subsequent government decisions placed the two bands on shared reserve land despite objections from members who had been away hunting. Ochapowace succeeded his father Kakisheway in 1884 as chief of the amalgamated bands. Their separate identities and the effects of that amalgamation are important to the community’s history; later land-claim developments require their own contemporary sources.

Okanese First Nation’s treaty record includes Chief Okanis, or Okanese, joining Treaty 4 on September 9, 1875 and settling in the File Hills. After his death, Moostooacoop served as headman until 1895. Members continued established ways of living while also developing gardens, crop farming and cattle herds as resources became scarce. Railway access at Balcarres in the early twentieth century created markets and employment. The community’s history also includes the File Hills Residential School, established in 1879 and closed in 1950. A treaty land entitlement framework agreement followed in December 1999.

One Arrow First Nation’s treaty record includes entry into Treaty 6 on September 6, 1878. The people settled on their reserve near the South Saskatchewan River in autumn 1880. The university account describes the site as suitable for agriculture and records the leadership of headman Crowskin in 1882, when the chief was elderly. The reserve period brought new forms of farming and settlement alongside older Cree relationships with the river country. The treaty date and reserve settlement are documented milestones, rather than a complete account of the people’s history.

Onion Lake Cree Nation’s history brings together the Seekaskootch and Makaoo bands. Seekaskootch’s people signed Treaty 6 at Fort Pitt on September 9, 1876, while the Makaoo band joined through an adhesion in 1878. Adjacent reserves followed in 1879. After 1885, federal officials classified both communities as rebellious and withheld recognition of a chief. In 1914, recognition was made conditional on amalgamation as the Onion Lake Band. Their reserve crosses the present Saskatchewan–Alberta boundary. These administrative events should be distinguished from the Cree communities’ earlier histories and from individual responsibility for events in 1885.

Pasqua First Nation’s treaty history includes Chief Joseph Pasqua signing Treaty 4 in September 1874. He selected land beside Pasqua Lake so his people could rely on fish and waterfowl when other game was scarce. Pasqua challenged inadequate treaty provisions and sought help for people facing hunger. After his death in 1889, the community petitioned for recognition of another chief; his son Ben was elected in 1911. A land surrender in 1906 later became the subject of a claim. The account records a diverse community and the effects of restrictive reserve administration.

Peepeekisis Cree Nation’s history includes Chief Can-ah-ha-cha-pew’s signing of Treaty 4 on September 21, 1874. His son Peepeekisis later became chief, and the people moved from the Cypress Hills to the File Hills in 1884. Beginning in 1898, Indian Agent W. M. Graham placed graduates from industrial schools on the reserve through the File Hills Colony scheme. Original members were displaced from homes and communal land. Complaints eventually led to a specific claim in 1986 and an Indian Claims Commission finding in 2004. This account concerns the historical scheme and does not describe the claim’s current status.

Pelican Lake First Nation’s history is associated with Cree families living near Pelican Lake and later Chitek Lake. The university account records entry into Treaty 6 in 1889 and continued hunting and fishing. Early department records associated the people with Kenemotayoo’s Big River band even while they lived separately. Reserve surveys and leadership arrangements developed over subsequent years. Louis Chamakee is recorded as the first chief. Farming supplemented other livelihoods, but trapping and wood sales remained important. This history distinguishes the community’s own settlement pattern from the administrative grouping used by officials.
connections: Early twentieth-century records associated Pelican Lake with Kenemotayoo’s Big River band and shared reserve ownership, despite separate residence.

summary: Peter Ballantyne Cree Nation’s documented treaty history is connected to the Lac La Ronge people’s adhesion to Treaty 6 on February 11, 1889. The university account places its ancestors within that earlier administrative grouping. The Nation’s land base encompasses several northern communities, including Pelican Narrows and Southend near Reindeer Lake, rather than a single settlement. Fishing, trapping and forestry feature prominently in the historical account of livelihoods. The treaty record describes a relationship with the Crown; it should not be taken as the beginning of Cree residence or as a complete explanation of the communities’ distinct histories.
connections: The university account connects Peter Ballantyne’s ancestors with the Lac La Ronge band’s 1889 Treaty 6 adhesion.

summary: Pheasant Rump Nakota Nation’s reserve history includes a Treaty 4 adhesion in 1876 and the granting of a reserve in 1881. Members farmed near Kisbey while also earning income from freighting, woodcutting and skilled work. In 1901, the band was amalgamated with White Bear after officials pursued surrender of its reserve. Descendants later sought restoration of their community and land base. A settlement agreement was signed in 1986, separate band recognition followed in 1990, and purchased land received reserve status in 1992. That restoration continued an older Nakota community history.
connections: Pheasant Rump was amalgamated with White Bear in 1901 before separate recognition was restored in 1990.

summary: Piapot Cree First Nation’s history includes Chief Piapot, also recorded as Payepot, joining Treaty 4 on September 9, 1875. He initially sought a reserve in the Cypress Hills. After pressure to relocate, the people settled beside Carry the Kettle in 1883, but a severe winter and many deaths led Piapot to seek another location. In September 1884, the band selected land northeast of Regina. Piapot’s resistance to official interference in ceremonies forms an important part of his leadership history. The successive reserve locations reflect displacement and negotiation, rather than the full extent of the people’s homeland.
connections: Piapot’s people briefly settled on a reserve bordering Carry the Kettle in 1883 before moving to another location.

summary: Poundmaker Cree Nation’s history includes the leadership of Pitikwahanapiwiyin, or Poundmaker, and the development of a separate band after his earlier association with Red Pheasant’s people. He participated in the Treaty 6 era and selected reserve land northwest of Battleford in 1881. Following his death, the band went without a recognized chief until 1920. His remains were returned to the reserve and buried at Cut Knife Hill in 1967. The university account also records later treaty land entitlement acquisitions. An inconsistent exact signing date in that entry is deliberately omitted here.
connections: Poundmaker was formerly associated with Red Pheasant’s band before leading a separate community.

summary: Red Earth Cree Nation’s history is rooted in the Carrot River district and the western Saskatchewan River delta. Late nineteenth-century settlements included families associated with Kiseyinis, or Little Old Man, and Cecim. The university account records their Treaty 5 adhesion on September 7, 1876, with reserves surveyed at Red Earth in 1884 and Carrot River in 1894. Hunting, fishing, gardens and livestock sustained families. Drought and declining fur resources in the 1930s, together with encroachment on hunting grounds, increased reliance on agriculture and paid work. These events concern adaptation within a much older Cree landscape.
detail: The university history identifies Treaty 5, whereas the existing profile dataset lists Treaty 6. The historical account is cited directly here; the existing profile classification has not been changed.

summary: Red Pheasant Cree Nation’s ancestors hunted, fished and traded along the Battle River before treaty. Chief Wuttunee, or Porcupine, opposed Treaty 6 and asked his brother Red Pheasant to sign on his behalf on September 9, 1876. Officials subsequently recognized Red Pheasant as chief. The people settled on their Eagle Hills reserve in 1878, where farmland and wooded areas supported their livelihoods. A day school opened in 1880 and an Anglican church followed in 1885. Later treaty land entitlement work expanded the reserve land base. The two brothers’ different roles are important to understanding the signing record.

Sakimay First Nations’ written treaty history includes Chief Sakimay, whose name also appears as Sah-ka-ma or Sah-kee-may, signing Treaty 4 on September 15, 1874. The reserve formed part of the western Crooked Lake reserve district. After the chief’s death, Yellow Calf acted as a spokesman in dealings with the Indian Agent during the early 1880s. The community’s land base includes the Sakimay, Shesheep, Little Bone and Minoahcuk reserves. Agriculture and later tourism appear in the historical account. The treaty record and reserve names capture only part of the people’s continuing history.

Saulteaux First Nation’s history includes a long-standing Treaty 6 land entitlement grievance and its eventual settlement. The university account records ratification of the Nation’s claim on April 7, 1993, enabling the purchase of additional agricultural, commercial, residential and other land in Saskatchewan. The community is described as Ojibway-speaking, with its main reserve settlement north of North Battleford. Its land claim concerned a treaty land debt, rather than the beginning of the Nation’s relationship with the land. The entry’s exact treaty date is not repeated here because it requires corroboration against the original adhesion records.

Shoal Lake Cree Nation’s history is rooted in the western Saskatchewan River delta, where Swampy Cree families lived during the nineteenth century. The university account identifies Okakeek, Osawask and Kis-moswakapaw among the community’s early recorded leaders and records a Treaty 5 adhesion in 1876. A reserve was surveyed in 1882. Gardening, livestock, hunting and fishing supported families, while later agricultural settlement nearby created markets and employment. Construction of an all-weather road in 1960–61 changed access to work and training. The village is also known as Pakwaw Lake.
detail: The university history identifies Treaty 5; the existing OpenBand profile dataset lists Treaty 6. This historical section preserves the source distinction without changing the other profile data.

summary: Standing Buffalo Dakota Nation’s history includes Tatankanaje becoming hereditary leader after his father’s death in 1871. The community received permission to farm north of the Qu’Appelle lakes in 1877, and a reserve was established there in 1881. Members developed farms and earned wages, but the small land allocation restricted growth. Repeated requests for more land included a journey to Ottawa by Standing Buffalo and his son Julius in 1920. Additional reserve acreage was not granted until 1956. These events describe a Dakota reserve history that should not be reduced to the treaty labels used elsewhere in the directory.

Star Blanket Cree Nation’s treaty history includes Chief Wah-pi-moos-toosis, or White Calf, joining Treaty 4 in 1874. His Calling River Cree people used territory extending through the File Hills, Wood Mountain and Cypress Hills. A reserve near Crooked Lake was surveyed in 1876, but the band did not settle there. Instead, it received land in the File Hills in 1880. Later land-claim work included transfer of the Lebret student residence in 1983 and Crown lots in Fort Qu’Appelle in 1994. These changes form part of the Nation’s reserve and land-recovery history.

Sturgeon Lake First Nation’s treaty-era record includes Chief Ah-yah-tus-kum-ik-im-am, also known as William Twatt, and four headmen signing Treaty 6 near Fort Carlton on August 23, 1876. A reserve at Sturgeon Lake followed in 1878. The community was long called the William Twatt Band before adopting the Sturgeon Lake name in 1963. Members combined farming and cattle raising with trapping, woodcutting and wage work. A grievance concerning timber revenue lost from 1906 was settled in 2001. This account concerns the Saskatchewan Nation and should not be confused with the separate Sturgeon Lake Cree Nation in Alberta.

Sweetgrass First Nation’s history includes Chief Weekaskookwasayin, or Sweet Grass, signing Treaty 6 with the Fort Pitt communities on September 9, 1876. Following his death, his son Apseenes, or Young Sweet Grass, succeeded him. Members later joined people led by Wah-wee-kah-oo-tah-mah-hote, another Treaty 6 signatory. A reserve west of Battleford was surveyed in 1884 for the combined community. Gardens, livestock and sales of hay and wood supported families during the reserve period. The history involves changing leadership and the coming together of groups, rather than a single founding event.

The Key First Nation’s people lived along the Shoal River in Manitoba before Chief Ow-tah-pee-ka-kaw, or The Key, signed a Treaty 4 adhesion on September 24, 1875. The band included families with Saulteaux, Cree and fur-trade connections. An initial reserve survey in 1878 was followed by relocation nearer Fort Pelly after flooding made the first site unsuitable. Skilled trades and agriculture helped families rebuild. Land surrenders in 1905 and 1909 reduced opportunities for agricultural expansion. The university account also records Gwen O’Soup’s election as chief in 1954, an important leadership milestone.

Wahpeton Dakota Nation’s ancestors used lands on both sides of the present Canada–United States border before settling near Prince Albert under Chief Hupa-yaktao in 1878. The community did not sign a numbered treaty. An Order in Council reserved land for it in 1894, with further acreage added in 1917 and 1930. Earlier Dakota encampments gradually combined their memberships. Farming later became important, although a limited land base constrained commercial development. Reserve creation was an administrative recognition within a much older Dakota history, rather than the beginning of the people’s existence or relationship with the region.

Waterhen Lake First Nation’s recorded treaty history includes an adhesion to Treaty 6 under Chief Running Around in January 1913. A reserve was surveyed in 1916. The chief sought assurance that the people could continue their established way of life. Hunting and trapping areas extended around Lost Lake and toward Primrose Lake. Provincial fur-conservation regulations later changed access, followed by establishment of the Primrose Lake Air Weapons Range in 1954. Members joined other communities in seeking compensation for lost harvesting lands during the 1970s. These events describe restrictions on an older land-based Cree economy.

White Bear First Nations’ history includes Chief Wahpemakwa, or White Bear, entering Treaty 4 in 1875 and accepting reserve land east of Moose Mountain in 1877. Members combined established livelihoods with agriculture. In 1901, officials amalgamated Ocean Man and Pheasant Rump onto White Bear’s reserve; a promised land extension followed only later and required payment by the band. Descendants of the affected communities eventually pursued claims concerning the surrendered reserves. Those separate band histories remain important when explaining White Bear’s past. The account should not imply that the amalgamation erased the identities of Ocean Man or Pheasant Rump.
connections: Ocean Man was amalgamated onto White Bear’s reserve in 1901 and later regained separate recognition.
Pheasant Rump was also amalgamated onto White Bear in 1901 before its separate band status was restored.

summary: Whitecap Dakota First Nation’s history includes Chief Wapahaska, or White Cap, and his people settling along the South Saskatchewan River. The community received a reserve in June 1881 without signing a numbered treaty. White Cap was tried after the 1885 Resistance and acquitted. Members returned to rebuild, developing cattle herds, farming and wage work. The university account describes later adaptation to changes in livestock markets. This is a history of a Dakota community with its own relationship to the Crown; a nearby treaty territory should not be mistaken for a treaty signed by Whitecap.

Witchekan Lake First Nation’s history includes land occupation and reserve surveys that preceded its formal Treaty 6 adhesion on November 21, 1950. The distinction matters because that relatively recent date does not mark the beginning of the Cree community. Agriculture, forestry, fishing and trapping feature in the university account of livelihoods. In 1997, the Nation acquired the Bapaume Community Pasture through a treaty land entitlement agreement. The acquisition expanded its land base and illustrates how treaty obligations continued to shape land recovery long after the original nineteenth-century Treaty 6 negotiations.

Wood Mountain First Nation’s Lakota history includes communities living and moving across the northern Plains before the present international boundary took its modern form. The university account describes settlement near Wood Mountain during the 1870s and the arrival of Sitting Bull’s followers. Some remained after he returned to the United States in 1881. They supported themselves through land-based livelihoods and wage work. A temporary reserve was created in 1910 and formally recognized in 1930. The people did not sign a numbered treaty with Canada; reserve recognition should not be presented as the beginning of Lakota presence in the region.

Yellow Quill First Nation’s treaty history includes Chief Yellow Quill and headmen Kenistin and Ne-Pin-awa signing a Treaty 4 adhesion at Fort Pelly on August 24, 1876. Reserve surveys at Fishing and Nut lakes followed in 1881, and Yellow Quill selected Nut Lake. Hunting, fishing and trapping continued before diminishing wildlife resources increased reliance on farming during the 1930s. Grain production became important in the following decades. A treaty land entitlement framework agreement was ratified on September 23, 1992. The historical Nut Lake identity and the wider treaty-era band should be distinguished from present-day administrative boundaries.

Kinistin Saulteaux Nation’s history includes movement from north of the Great Lakes into the Qu’Appelle Valley with Yellow Quill’s people. Their Treaty 4 adhesion was signed at Fort Pelly on August 24, 1876. Kinistin later led a separate community in the Barrier River district. The people moved north during the upheaval of 1885, then returned to seek reserve land. With assistance from Reginald Beatty, a reserve was established in 1900. The university account explains that Kinistino was a clerical rendering of Kinistin’s name. The community’s separate identity should be distinguished from that administrative spelling.
connections: Kinistin’s people were historically associated with Yellow Quill before developing a separate community in the Barrier River district.

summary: George Gordon First Nation’s history includes an enduring Treaty 4 land entitlement grievance. The Nation’s own account explains that some people were absent when the treaty census was taken, leaving a shortfall in the reserve land allocated under the treaty’s population-based formula. A settlement agreement was ratified on February 15, 2008 and became effective on August 11 that year. Canada and Saskatchewan provided compensation toward land acquisition, with settlement funds held under specified trust conditions. This land-recovery history concerns an outstanding treaty obligation, rather than the beginning of the Nation or its relationship with the territory.

Thunderchild First Nation’s treaty history includes an adhesion to Treaty 6 in August 1879, several years after the original negotiations. The Nation’s agricultural benefits claim information records that its people were initially required to live on Moosomin’s reserve. The treaty promised livestock, tools, seed and agricultural instruction, but the Nation’s account describes those obligations as inadequately fulfilled. Its later claim sought redress for that history. The distinction between the 1876 treaty negotiations and Thunderchild’s 1879 adhesion is important; neither date represents the beginning of the Cree community’s existence.
connections: Thunderchild’s claim history records that members were required to live on Moosomin’s reserve after adhering to Treaty 6.

summary: English River Dene Nation’s history is associated with the Poplar House People and families who lived around Primeau, Knee, Cree and Dipper lakes before gathering at Patuanak. Meadow Lake Tribal Council identifies William Apesis as the chief at the 1906 signing of Treaty 10. The community’s earlier reserve name was Grassy Narrows. Fishing, hunting and gathering along the Churchill River remained important as settlement and educational institutions changed. An elementary school opened in 1971 and a high school was completed in 2000. These developments form part of the Nation’s history without defining the beginning of Dene occupation of the region.

Fishing Lake First Nation describes itself as an Anishnabe community with roots in the wider Saulteaux and Ojibway world. Its own history connects the people with movement into the Qu’Appelle Valley during the nineteenth century and with Chief Yellow Quill’s Treaty 4 adhesion. That earlier group included people who later formed distinct communities at Fishing Lake, Nut Lake and under Kinistin. The account emphasizes those relationships and the leadership involved in the westward and northward movements. It does not make the treaty the beginning of Anishnabe existence, and uncertain details about Yellow Quill’s birthplace are not treated as settled fact here.
connections: Fishing Lake’s own history links its treaty-era community with Yellow Quill’s people at Nut Lake.
The Nation’s history identifies Kinistin as a leader within the wider Yellow Quill treaty-era group.

summary: Flying Dust First Nation’s own history connects Chief Kopahawakenum and the people around Green Lake with Treaty 6 and later settlement near Meadow Lake. Its account records the historical name Green Lake Indians in annuity lists and describes kinship with neighbouring Cree communities. Hunting, trapping and fishing supported families before the reserve pass system and declining resources encouraged greater reliance on agriculture. The Nation also records the withholding of annuities after officials wrongly classified its people as rebels in 1885. Railway land taken in 1932 later became the subject of a specific claim. Conflicting exact treaty dates on the page are omitted.

Birch Narrows Dene Nation’s community plan places its history in the Clear Lake region since time immemorial. Chief Raphael, whose name appears in several transliterations, signed Treaty 10 for the Clear Lake Band at Île-à-la-Crosse on August 28, 1906. Later records use the Peter Pond Lake Band name. Many members relocated in 1965, and Turnor Lake was recognized as a separate band in 1972. It adopted the Birch Narrows Dene Nation name in 1990. These administrative changes belong to a continuing Denesuline history; they should not be presented as the origin of the people or their homeland.
connections: Birch Narrows and Buffalo River share the earlier Peter Pond Band history; the communities became separate bands in 1972.

publisher: University of Regina · Encyclopedia of Saskatchewan
summary: Fond du Lac Denesuline First Nation’s treaty-era history includes joining Treaty 8 in July 1899 as part of Maurice Piche’s band. Hunting, fishing and trapping continued across a broad northern territory. The encyclopedia describes efforts during the 1930s and 1940s to secure reserve land in northeastern Saskatchewan and the Northwest Territories. On January 11, 1960, Indian Affairs acknowledged an outstanding treaty land entitlement and allowed land selections. The community on Lake Athabasca therefore has a history that extends well beyond the timing of reserve recognition and the boundaries drawn in federal records.
connections: Fond du Lac and Black Lake share the earlier Maurice Piche band history before their formal administrative division.

summary: Alexander First Nation, Kipohtakaw, describes a Cree history rooted in the forests, lakes and rivers of central Alberta long before European contact. The Nation takes its English name from Chief Catchistahwayskum, or Alexander, who signed a Treaty 6 adhesion in 1877. Its own account emphasizes continuity through Cree language, ceremonies and spiritual teachings, rather than treating the treaty as a founding date. Land and water stewardship remain part of that relationship with the territory. The history of reserve administration is therefore one chapter within a much longer history of the people around present-day Morinville.

Alexis Nakota Sioux Nation’s own history centres on Mitaushin Aranazhi, Stands On Top, whose treaty-government name was recorded as Chief Alexis Kees-kee-chee-chi. He signed the Treaty 6 adhesion on August 21, 1877. The Nation recounts the ceremony, songs and teachings associated with the people’s journey to Fort Edmonton, preserving an oral account alongside the written record. Although Indian Affairs recognized a limited period of formal office, the community continued to recognize his leadership until his death in 1913. This distinction illustrates why government appointment records alone cannot represent Nakota governance and history.

Athabasca Chipewyan First Nation identifies its people as K’ai Tailé Dené, people of the land of the willow. Its history is rooted in the Peace–Athabasca Delta, where hunting, trapping, fishing and gathering sustained families over many generations. The Nation signed Treaty 8 at Fort Chipewyan in 1899. Its own account presents that agreement within an existing cultural and territorial relationship, rather than as the beginning of the community. Dene language, inherited knowledge and responsibility for the delta remain central to the Nation’s explanation of its past and its continuing treaty relationship.

Bearspaw First Nation describes a traditional territory extending from buffalo-hunting country on the Plains through the Rocky Mountain foothills and watersheds, across passes into present-day British Columbia. Chief Jacob Bearspaw, Ozija Thiba, signed Treaty 7 at Blackfoot Crossing on September 22, 1877. The Nation’s history connects it with Chiniki and Goodstoney while preserving the distinct identity of each. Stoney Nakoda language and place names carry knowledge of rivers, mountains and travel routes. The treaty and reserve lands form part of that story, within a much older Îyârhe Nakoda relationship with the mountains and Plains.
connections: Bearspaw and Chiniki are distinct Stoney Nakoda communities whose chiefs participated in Treaty 7.
Bearspaw’s history identifies Goodstoney as a fellow Stoney Nakoda Treaty 7 signatory.

summary: Beaver First Nation is a Dane-zaa community whose history is associated with the Fort Vermilion, Boyer River and Child Lake areas. Its community app information records Chief Ambroise Tête Noire joining Treaty 8 at Fort Vermilion on July 8, 1899. Historical administrative names included the Fort Vermilion Band of Beaver Indians and Boyer River Band before adoption of the present name in 1992. The people’s territory and land-based livelihoods extended beyond the two reserves. Dane-zaa language and Elders’ knowledge remain important records of a history older than the treaty and the band names used by officials.

Beaver Lake Cree Nation’s own history identifies the people as Wood Cree with longstanding connections to the Lac La Biche region. Chief Pee-Yas-See-Wah-We-Cha-Koot, also known as Pee-ay-sis, and councillor Pay-Pay-See-See-Moo signed Treaty 6 at Fort Pitt on September 9, 1876. Reserve land was not formally set apart until May 31, 1911. The Nation describes declining fish and game, epidemics and pressure to change established livelihoods during the intervening period. It also records people joining from the Lac La Biche band. These events concern treaty obligations and colonial administration within an older Cree history.

Bigstone Cree Nation joined Treaty 8 in 1899, but outstanding obligations concerning reserve land and other benefits continued for more than a century. A settlement approved in community votes in 2010 addressed treaty land entitlement and ancillary benefits. The process included members from Wabasca, Calling Lake, Chipewyan Lake, Peerless Lake and Trout Lake. One result was the separate constitution of Peerless Trout First Nation on May 19, 2010. These administrative developments did not create the communities’ Indigenous histories; they addressed aspects of an existing treaty relationship and the distinct needs of people living across the region.
connections: Peerless Trout became a separate First Nation through the Bigstone treaty land entitlement and benefits settlement process in 2010.

summary: The Blood Tribe, or Kainai, describes its relationship with the Crown through the Blackfoot Treaty of 1877, commonly called Treaty 7. Its own account explains the agreement through Innaihtsiiyissini, a Blackfoot understanding of treaty-making as a peace relationship between powerful nations. That perspective places the agreement within an existing political and cultural order, rather than treating it as the beginning of the Tribe. The Nation’s history and interpretation of treaty belong to the wider Blackfoot world while retaining a distinct Kainai identity. This account summarizes that historical relationship without turning present-day political statements into historical facts.

Chiniki First Nation describes its people as Îyârhe Nakoda, people of the mountains, with a history of travel across the foothills and Rocky Mountain slopes into present-day Montana and British Columbia. Hunting buffalo and other game, fishing and harvesting plants were guided by land-based knowledge and ceremony. Chief John Chiniki joined Jacob Bearspaw and Jacob Goodstoney at the Treaty 7 negotiations at Blackfoot Crossing in 1877. Reserve creation later reshaped access to parts of that territory. Chiniki’s account preserves a distinct community history within the shared Stoney Nakoda world.
connections: Chiniki and Bearspaw are distinct Stoney Nakoda Nations whose chiefs signed Treaty 7 together.
Chiniki’s history identifies Jacob Goodstoney as another Stoney Nakoda chief at the 1877 negotiations.

summary: Chipewyan Prairie First Nation’s own account locates its Denésoliné history in lands radiating outward from the Christina River watershed. Hunting, gathering and other land-based activities sustained the people’s livelihood, culture and identity long before reserve administration. The reserve at Janvier is adjacent to the separate hamlet of Janvier, which also includes Métis families and other residents. These neighbouring places should not be treated as a single government or as having identical histories. The Nation describes Denésoliné as its inherited language and emphasizes continuity of land use rather than a single founding event.

Cold Lake First Nations’ own historical account, including a narrative by John N. A. Janvier, places Denesųłiné presence far earlier than written colonial records. The Nation describes land, language, stories and teachings as inseparable, with Elders responsible for passing knowledge between generations. Its history includes the effects of imposed reserve administration and restrictions on movement, alongside the continuation of community relationships across the wider territory. The account emphasizes that land sustained the people for thousands of years. This brief preserves that perspective rather than reducing Cold Lake’s history to a treaty date or a government-created boundary.

Dene Tha’ First Nation’s published history draws on its 1997 Traditional Land-Use and Occupancy Study. Elders’ accounts describe hunting, trapping, fishing, gathering and the rules for using land responsibly. Knowledge passed through family relationships and storytelling, rather than depending solely on written records. Around the turn of the twentieth century, trading posts and log houses contributed to more settled patterns of residence, while land-based life remained important. The study records both continuing occupation and change. Its account should therefore be read as a history told through Dene Tha’ knowledge, alongside the later administrative record.

Driftpile Cree Nation’s history is connected to Lesser Slave Lake and Chief Kinosayo’s participation in Treaty 8 in 1899. The Nation’s own timeline describes later administrative divisions of the original band and the importance of gardens, farming and household work in community life. George Okimaw is remembered for teaching agricultural practices. Women’s work included preparing hides and clothing, caring for children and managing essential household needs. These details broaden the written treaty record into a history of families and livelihoods. Uncertain stories about reserve boundaries on the source page are not repeated as established fact here.

Duncan’s First Nation’s own history records entry into Treaty 8 on July 1, 1899. Reserve parcels were surveyed in 1905, with formal confirmations in 1907 and 1925. Most were surrendered in 1928; one parcel, 151K, was returned in 1965. These land changes are central to the community’s reserve history in the Peace River region. The account also records later regional relationships, including formation of the Western Cree Tribal Council in 1998 with Horse Lake and Sturgeon Lake. The people’s Woods Cree history extends beyond those treaty, land and organizational dates.
connections: Duncan’s and Horse Lake formed the Western Cree Tribal Council with Sturgeon Lake in 1998.
Duncan’s history records a shared role with Sturgeon Lake in forming the Western Cree Tribal Council in 1998.

summary: Enoch Cree Nation’s own account records joining Treaty 6 on September 25, 1877. Its people identify with Plains Cree history and with the land west of present-day Edmonton. Stony Plain Reserve 135 was established in September 1889. The Nation describes land losses in 1902 and 1908 as forced sales and wrongful surrenders that substantially reduced its land base. Language, stories, songs, dance and ceremony preserve an identity older than those administrative events. The treaty is presented as a nation-to-nation relationship with the Crown, rather than the origin of the community.

Ermineskin Cree Nation’s own history places its people in the Bear Hills, Maskwacheesihk, for centuries before the reserve was established in 1885. It identifies Ermineskin as one of the Four Sister Nations of Maskwacis and as part of Treaty 6. The account emphasizes the continuation of Cree community identity through language, culture and the preservation of history. Agricultural land and later oil and gas resources became important in reserve-era economic life. The 1885 reserve date is an administrative milestone within that older history, not the beginning of the Nation’s connection with the Bear Hills.

Fort McKay First Nation’s history is rooted in Cree and Dene communities along the Athabasca River and surrounding lakes. Its own account notes the Hudson’s Bay Company trading post established near the present community in 1820, a point in the written fur-trade record rather than the start of Indigenous occupation. Fort McKay is a Treaty 8 Nation. The community’s land base also includes places at Moose and Buffalo lakes, reflecting relationships beyond the main settlement. More recent industry relationships form another chapter in a history that includes land-based livelihoods and distinct Cree and Dene heritage.

publisher: Indian Claims Commission · Government of Canada
summary: Fort McMurray #468 First Nation’s treaty-era history includes the federal creation of the Fort McMurray Cree-Chipewyan Band in 1899. The Indian Claims Commission’s inquiry explains that this grouping was administratively convenient and did not correspond to a single pre-existing community. Cree and Dene groups associated with Fort McMurray, Fort McKay and other locations retained distinct residence and land-use histories. The Treaty 8 adhesion and subsequent band administration therefore need to be distinguished from the people’s earlier identities. This account avoids treating a shared government record as proof of identical language, ancestry or governance.
connections: Fort McKay and Fort McMurray were historically administered within the Fort McMurray Cree-Chipewyan Band, despite distinct community identities.

summary: Frog Lake’s nineteenth-century history includes the severe pressures faced by Plains Cree communities after Treaty 6: disappearing bison, hunger and government withholding of promised assistance. Alberta’s historic-site account explains the killings at Frog Lake in 1885 within that wider context. It also notes that more recent research and oral histories have changed interpretations of the event. Chief Big Bear sought improved conditions and fulfilment of treaty promises. The tragedy should not be used to assign collective responsibility to today’s Frog Lake First Nation or to replace the community’s much broader history with one episode.

facts.Historical pressures: Bison decline, hunger and withheld assistance

summary: Goodstoney First Nation’s account of Goodstoney Meadows describes a gathering place used by Stoney Nakoda families since time immemorial. Families and clans returned from winter camps in spring to meet, share food and stories, and welcome warmer weather. The meadows also hosted horse racing, sports and ceremonies, including the Sundance. This seasonal gathering history connects the community with the wider Rocky Mountain landscape and with knowledge preserved through ceremony and oral tradition. It provides a different kind of historical record from treaty signatures or reserve surveys, without making those colonial documents the starting point of the people’s story.

publisher: Portage College · Lac La Biche Archives
summary: Heart Lake First Nation’s written treaty history contains conflicting administrative records. The Lac La Biche Archives’ historical study explains that federal registers variously associated Heart Lake with Treaty 6 and Treaty 8, while a recorded 1899 date was inconsistent with the actual start of Treaty 8 negotiations. A 1916 Order in Council set aside reserve land under Treaty 8 terms. The study cautions that the precise signing history is not established by those records alone. This brief preserves that uncertainty rather than assigning a confident signing date, and distinguishes administrative classification from the community’s older history.

publisher: British Columbia Environmental Assessment Office · consultation record
summary: Horse Lake First Nation’s history is connected to Dane-zaa people and a territory extending across present-day northwestern Alberta and northeastern British Columbia. The provincial consultation record identifies its predecessor as the Beaver Band at Dunvegan, which adhered to Treaty 8 on July 6, 1899. Hunting, fishing, trapping and cultural practices continued across a wider area than the reserve boundaries. The account records Dane-zaa as a traditional language. These treaty-era names describe colonial administration and should not be taken as a complete account of the community’s ancestry, oral histories or land relationships.

Kapawe’no First Nation’s community history is associated with Grouard in the Lesser Slave Lake region. Its own account describes a governance tradition based on hereditary leadership and remembers Frank Halcrow’s fifty years as chief, beginning in 1970 and ending with his death in January 2020. The Nation also records the development of a governance plan defining leadership responsibilities. Education includes Cree language instruction and land-based teaching, connecting institutional development with inherited knowledge. These documented leadership and educational developments form part of the Nation’s modern history; the present reserve system does not define the beginning of the people’s connection with the area.

publisher: Elk Point Historical Society · account by former Chief Theresa Gadwa
summary: Kehewin Cree Nation’s history is recounted by former Chief Theresa Gadwa in an account preserved by the Elk Point Historical Society. She places the community’s treaty-era establishment in 1876 and describes how the reserve system changed Cree freedom of movement and political life. Her account explains the roles of the Okimaw, or chief, and councillors in dealings with Indian Affairs. It presents treaty and reserve administration as changes imposed on an existing people, rather than their origin. The perspective of a former community leader adds an important voice alongside government documents.

Little Red River Cree Nation’s treaty record includes joining Treaty 8 at the Little Red River post on July 11, 1899. The first annuity distribution there took place on the same day. North Peace Tribal Council’s account emphasizes that the Nation’s unwritten history reaches much further back and has been passed between generations through collective storytelling. Its communities include Fox Lake, John D’or Prairie and Garden River. Treaty documentation and present-day administrative arrangements therefore describe only part of a wider Cree history. Oral knowledge and the records of the different communities remain important in understanding that past.

Loon River First Nation’s own history distinguishes the wider Treaty 8 relationship, dating to 1899, from the community’s later achievement of reserve status in 1993. Its account presents reserve recognition as a milestone in self-government and Nation-building, not the beginning of the people’s existence. Language, culture, Christian traditions and responsibility for traditional lands are identified as important parts of the community’s inherited identity. The history of formal recognition must therefore be read alongside a much older pattern of community life and land use. An exact individual adhesion date is not assigned from the general Treaty 8 date.

Louis Bull Tribe’s history belongs to the Cree communities of Maskwacis, the Bear Hills region of central Alberta. The Tribe identifies itself as one of the Four Nations of Maskwacis. Its own public account connects the reserve system with the treaty period while emphasizing a continuing Cree community identity. More recent economic history includes the Tribe’s founding and ownership of the Bear Hills Casino and Travel Resort. That development is part of a broader effort to support employment and community services. It is a modern chapter in the Tribe’s story, rather than an explanation of the origins of its people.

facts.Modern community enterprise: Bear Hills Casino and Travel Resort

publisher: Crown-Indigenous Relations and Northern Affairs Canada
summary: Lubicon Lake Band’s modern land history includes decades of negotiation over an unresolved land claim and treaty benefits. In October 2018, the Band, Alberta and Canada announced signed agreements following a community vote supporting settlement. The agreements provided a substantial land allocation, compensation and support for community infrastructure. This settlement addressed longstanding outstanding obligations; it should not be described as the beginning of the Lubicon people or their relationship with their territory. The history also demonstrates why residence inside the geographical area of Treaty 8 does not, by itself, establish an original 1899 signing date for every community.

facts.Significant agreement: Land claim and treaty benefits settlement
facts.Parties: Lubicon Lake Band, Alberta and Canada

summary: Mikisew Cree First Nation’s treaty history includes joining Treaty 8 in 1899. Its traditional territory lies largely in northeastern Alberta, where land and resource decisions have repeatedly affected the exercise of treaty rights. The Nation later challenged federal law-making that it argued could affect those rights. A Supreme Court of Canada decision in October 2018 considered the Crown’s obligations during the legislative process. That case is part of the modern history of the Nation’s defence of its treaty relationship, rather than a replacement for its older community history or an account of all its legal proceedings.

Montana First Nation’s history is rooted in Maskwacis, the Bear Hills, where Cree people gathered for social and spiritual purposes before the treaty period. The Nation’s own account explains that land initially set aside for Bobtail’s band was later granted to the Montana Band after the earlier residents dispersed. A surrender in 1909 greatly reduced that reserve. The account connects this land history with Treaty 6 and the choices made around reserve settlement. Its discussion of the surrender is a historical account; the present status of any related litigation is not inferred from an undated website statement.

O’Chiese First Nation’s own oral-history account describes Saulteaux movement westward during the fur-trade period and families using the Baptiste River as a winter camp. Hunting and trapping supported families who also travelled south in summer. Elders’ accounts connect settlement in the area with efforts to keep children from residential schools. In 1950, a group of families joined Treaty 6 and settled on reserve land near Rocky Mountain House. The community identifies Saulteaux and Cree ancestry and Saulteaux language. These oral accounts place the twentieth-century treaty adhesion within a much older history of movement and land use.

Paul First Nation’s own account describes Nakoda movement over a broad territory from the Hudson Bay region toward the Rocky Mountains and south along the foothills. Connections with Cree people and participation in the fur trade formed part of that movement. One of the Stoney groups later chose land northwest of present-day Edmonton and became associated with Paul First Nation. This account emphasizes the wider landscape and relationships that preceded the reserve community. It should not be read as fixing every family’s ancestry or reducing the history of the people to a single migration, treaty or reserve date.

Peerless Trout First Nation’s community history is rooted in the lakes, muskeg and prairies around Peerless and Trout lakes. Fish and wildlife sustained families well before the modern band was constituted. The Nation was officially constituted on May 19, 2010 as part of the wider Bigstone land and treaty-benefits settlement process. Its own account explains that recognition in relation to the communities’ long struggle for land and services. The 2010 date concerns separate band administration; it does not mark the beginning of the people, their Cree identity or their relationship with the surrounding traditional territory.
connections: Peerless Trout’s separate band recognition arose through the Bigstone treaty land entitlement and benefits settlement.

summary: Piikani Nation’s own account places its history within the Blackfoot Confederacy and a territory sustained by stories, ceremonies, songs and detailed land knowledge. It describes an ancestral landscape reaching north toward the North Saskatchewan River, south toward the Yellowstone country and through the Rocky Mountains. The Nation presents itself as a continuing custodian of that territory, rather than a community created by a colonial boundary. Its intergovernmental charter records that historical understanding and the responsibility to preserve knowledge across generations. This territorial account represents the Nation’s own perspective and is not presented as an exclusive modern boundary map.

Saddle Lake Cree Nation’s own timeline records nineteenth-century leaders including Kehkek and Onchaminahos, or Little Hunter, and their participation in Treaty 6 in 1876. It also records the legal amalgamation of Blue Quills, Saddle Lake, Waskatenaw and Whitefish lands in 1902. The community’s later history includes a 1925 land surrender, residential schooling, restrictions on movement and the development of local institutions. The component communities’ histories should not be erased by the administrative amalgamation. Dates on the source timeline that are inconsistent with established wider chronology are not repeated here.
connections: ab-whitefish-lake-128
Whitefish and Saddle Lake were included in the 1902 land amalgamation recorded by Saddle Lake; their present community identities remain distinct.

publisher: Nipisihkopahk Iyinisiwin Trust Fund · Samson Cree Nation
summary: Samson Cree Nation’s modern history includes a sustained community investment in education. On June 23, 1980, Chief and Council established the Nipisihkopahk Iyinisiwin Trust Fund and set aside funds to support members’ educational goals. The trust’s own history explains that later leadership continued that commitment. This institutional history records a deliberate community choice to support future generations through education. It is one part of the Nation’s broader Cree history and should not be mistaken for a founding date or a complete account of its land, treaty and cultural relationships.

Sawridge First Nation’s own account records Chief Charles Neesotasis, also called Twin, signing Treaty 8 on the shores of Lesser Slave Lake on June 21, 1899. Its name refers to the ridged landscape of its homeland. The Nation places the treaty within a community history extending back long before the written agreement. More recent history includes economic development beginning in the early 1970s and efforts to strengthen self-determination. Neesotasis is remembered for seeking opportunities for descendants and maintaining the community’s future. The account presents treaty as an enduring relationship rather than an isolated historical transaction.

Siksika Nation’s own history describes the Siksikaitsitapi, or Blackfoot people, living across a large Plains territory since time immemorial. Its account extends that landscape from the North Saskatchewan River south toward the Yellowstone River and from the Continental Divide east into present-day Saskatchewan. Siksika is one of the distinct Nations of the Blackfoot Confederacy, alongside Kainai, Northern Piikani and Southern Piikani. Language and relationships across that territory preserve a history older than the current international boundary. This brief records that shared historical context while retaining Siksika’s separate identity and governance.
connections: Siksika’s own account identifies Kainai, or Blood Tribe, as a distinct member of the Blackfoot Confederacy.
Northern Piikani is identified as another distinct Blackfoot Confederacy Nation.

publisher: Crown-Indigenous Relations and Northern Affairs Canada
summary: Sturgeon Lake Cree Nation’s treaty history includes an adhesion to Treaty 8 at Lesser Slave Lake on June 8, 1900. Commissioner James Ansdell Macrae recorded meeting Cree people from Sturgeon Lake who wished to enter the treaty. His report distinguishes this adhesion from the original treaty negotiations of 1899. These documents preserve a Crown account of the encounter and the formal agreement. They do not establish the beginning of Cree history in the region. Later regional cooperation included the formation of the Western Cree Tribal Council with Duncan’s and Horse Lake First Nations in 1998.
connections: Duncan’s history records the three Nations forming the Western Cree Tribal Council in 1998.
Horse Lake shared in forming the Western Cree Tribal Council with Sturgeon Lake and Duncan’s in 1998.
extra_sources: Duncan’s First Nation — regional council history
