Commissioner James Ansdell Macrae recorded meeting Cree people from Sturgeon Lake who wished to enter the treaty. His report distinguishes this adhesion from the original treaty negotiations of 1899. These documents preserve a Crown account of the encounter and the formal agreement. They do not establish the beginning of Cree history in the region.
Later regional cooperation included the formation of the Western Cree Tribal Council with Duncan’s and Horse Lake First Nations in 1998.

summary: Sucker Creek First Nation, Namipi Sipîsis, describes its Cree history in the Lesser Slave Lake region and its Treaty 8 relationship dating to 1899. Its own account emphasizes kinship, language and shared experience. The history also includes the effects of St. Bruno’s Residential School at Joussard, attended by many members before its closure, and later changes in schooling. Those experiences belong within a continuing community history rather than defining the Nation only through colonial institutions. The present reserve near Kinuso is one part of a wider Nehiyaw relationship with the land and the lake.

Sunchild First Nation’s own account records its Treaty 6 adhesion on May 25, 1944 under Chief Louis Sunchild. The community’s reserve, Sunchild 202, lies northwest of Rocky Mountain House and adjoins O’Chiese. The relatively recent adhesion and reserve administration should not be mistaken for the beginning of the Cree families or their relationship with the region. The source describes a continuing community with its own educational and local institutions. This brief distinguishes the specific Sunchild adhesion from the original Treaty 6 negotiations held decades earlier in 1876.

Swan River First Nation’s own historical account describes Woodland Cree families around the south shore of Lesser Slave Lake. Summer lakeside settlements were connected with inland hunting and trapping camps. The people participated in the Treaty 8 process in 1899, alongside other Lesser Slave Lake communities. Fur trading, farming and changing wildlife resources shaped livelihoods during that period. The account identifies settlements at Swan River, Wahpah and Assineau River, placing the reserve community within a wider seasonal landscape. Treaty and reserve boundaries therefore record only part of the history of movement and land use.

facts.Historical region: South shore of Lesser Slave Lake

summary: Tallcree Tribal Government’s own account places Woodland Cree families along the Peace River and in the northern boreal forest over many generations. Seasonal movement, hunting, fishing and trapping sustained community life and Cree teachings. Tallcree joined Treaty 8 in 1899. The account describes subsequent disruption from settlement, government restrictions and residential schools, alongside the persistence of identity. South Tallcree near Fort Vermilion became the first recognized reserve community; families later moved north closer to traplines, forming North Tallcree. These administrative and settlement changes sit within an older history of land use.

Tsuut’ina Nation’s own account emphasizes a distinct Dene-speaking identity connected with a wider history of language, culture, customs and territory. The people were formerly called Sarcee or Sarsi in colonial records. Head Chief Chiila, or Bullhead, entered Treaty 7 with the Crown in 1877. The Nation interprets that relationship through its own laws and teachings while maintaining the autonomy of its identity and governance. Oral histories explain the people’s earlier movement and relationships. The treaty date therefore belongs within a continuing Tsuut’ina history rather than marking the origin of the Nation.

publisher: Town of Fort Smith · community profile
summary: Tthebatthie Denesųłiné Nation, historically recorded as Smith’s Landing First Nation, is connected with the Thebathi Dénésųłiné of the South Slave region. The Fort Smith community profile identifies the people as Treaty 8 signatories with longstanding use of lands and waters across the northern region. Its account describes Dene Ch’anié, the path we walk, as a guide to conduct and responsibility toward the land. Reserve lands lie in Alberta and Wood Buffalo National Park, while community relationships also extend into Fort Smith. Modern provincial and territorial boundaries do not contain the whole of this history.

publisher: University of Saskatchewan thesis · Library and Archives Canada
summary: Whitefish Lake First Nation at Atikameg has a treaty history that requires care with the distinction between signing and administration. A historical study of communities left out of the original Treaty 8 process records Whitefish Lake people appearing on the 1901 annuity paylist and receiving arrears for earlier years. The study notes uncertainty about representation at the original negotiations and the absence of a designated chief or headman in those records. This account therefore does not assign a confident 1899 signing date. Whitefish Lake 459 is distinct from Whitefish Lake 128 at Goodfish Lake.

publisher: Whitefish Lake First Nation #128 · impact-assessment submission
summary: Whitefish Lake First Nation #128’s own historical submission describes ancestors occupying the North Saskatchewan River watershed before European arrival. Families hunted, trapped and fished under their own laws and customs. During the fur trade, they interacted with traders at places including Fort Edmonton and Fort Augustus near the Sturgeon River’s mouth. The account connects the present Goodfish Lake community with that wider land-use history, rather than restricting its past to the reserve boundary. Whitefish Lake 128 should be distinguished from Whitefish Lake 459 at Atikameg, despite their similar English names.

Woodland Cree First Nation’s own account records signing a Treaty 8 adhesion on September 24, 1991. Its communities and reserve lands are associated with Cadotte, Simon, Golden and Marten lakes northeast of Peace River. The comparatively recent treaty adhesion belongs to the history of formal recognition and community administration, rather than the beginning of the people’s Cree identity or relationship with the region. The Nation describes a commitment to a self-supporting community that respects people, the environment and neighbouring communities. Its several settlements should not be reduced to a single village or treated as newly created by the adhesion.

facts.Historical communities: Cadotte, Simon, Golden and Marten lakes

summary: Barren Lands First Nation is associated with Brochet and Reserve 197 on the northern shore of Reindeer Lake. Keewatin Tribal Council identifies Cree and Dene as the community’s Indigenous languages and records its Treaty 10 relationship. Part of the earlier Barren Lands band later separated to form Northlands First Nation and moved to Lac Brochet, farther north. This shared administrative history helps explain the relationship between the two present-day Nations. The division of a band and the establishment of reserves are milestones in government records, rather than the beginning of the peoples’ relationship with the Reindeer Lake region.
connections: Northlands separated from the earlier Barren Lands band and relocated to Lac Brochet.

summary: Berens River’s recent history includes a sustained effort to bring education services under community direction. Its Student Services account traces the initiative to 2003, when Chief Alfred Everett began proceedings to transfer services from Southeast Tribal Council. Chief Nancy Everett subsequently negotiated and signed the transfer agreements. The Nation describes this as a step toward self-governance. Its account also recalls the sacrifices of families whose children had to leave home to continue secondary school. This history of education and community responsibility forms one part of Berens River’s broader story, preserved through the Mino-Kii-Kii-mah ghe-win documentary.

Birdtail Sioux identifies itself as Chan Kagha Otina Dakhóta Oyáte, a Dakota Nation with an ancestral connection to its territory. Its own historical timeline distinguishes that relationship from the later Canadian administration of reserve lands. On January 4, 1873, an Order in Council authorized lands to be set aside for Dakota communities, including Birdtail Sioux. The Nation’s account emphasizes that this did not constitute a treaty with Canada. Its history therefore should not be presented as a numbered-treaty signing story. The timeline also records later community development, including the opening of a health centre in 2009.

Black River First Nation appears in earlier federal records as the Little Black River Band. A Canada Gazette order records that its council had been placed under Indian Act election provisions in March 1952. A band council resolution dated September 7, 2005 changed the name to Black River First Nation. In March 2017 the council requested a move to the First Nations Elections Act, followed by the federal order registered that May. These documented changes describe the history of the Nation’s official name and election framework; they do not mark the origin of the community or its Indigenous identity.

Bloodvein River First Nation describes generations of Anishinaabe life along the river, where fishing, hunting, gathering and travel sustained families. The Nation records that Sakachewayas signed Treaty 5 as Chief of Bloodvein on July 26, 1876. Its history names the Stomach (Green), Skye (Young), Benson, Turtle and Swift families among those recorded in the late nineteenth century. Elders’ teachings and seasonal harvesting continue to connect members with this history. Through its Miskwewesibi Roots Program, the Nation gathers photographs, family histories and community stories so that this knowledge can be carried forward to younger generations.

Brokenhead Ojibway Nation identifies itself as an Ojibway community and a Treaty 1 Nation. Its reserve extends toward Lake Winnipeg and includes part of the Netley Creek marsh area, with the Brokenhead River running through the community. The Nation’s published vision places Ojibway identity alongside community independence and development. Its treaty relationship belongs to the history of Treaty 1, originally signed at Lower Fort Garry on August 3, 1871. That agreement is a historical milestone within a much longer Indigenous history. The river, lake and marsh remain important geographical context for understanding the community’s place in southeastern Manitoba.

summary: Buffalo Point’s own history describes the Point and Reed River as gathering places and travel routes used by Anishinaabe people. Chief Ayashwash signed Treaty 3 for Buffalo Point at the Northwest Angle in 1873. Flooding in 1890 affected the reserve; a later exchange for lands at Reed River was completed in 1930. The Nation’s account follows successive generations of Thunder family leadership and the development of tourism during the 1970s. These events connect the treaty period, changes to the land base and later economic development. They form a selected account of a community whose relationship with the area predates the treaty.

Bunibonibee Cree Nation’s published community history includes Oxford House’s role in the fur trade. Manitoba Keewatinowi Okimakanak describes the establishment of a Hudson’s Bay Company post there in 1798 and the later influence of the United Church. These are milestones in the written history of the settlement, rather than the beginning of Cree life in the region. Keewatin Tribal Council records Bunibonibee’s adhesion to Treaty 5 in 1909. The community is associated with Oxford Lake and the Hayes River, waterways that help explain its position within the northern trading and transportation network.

summary: Canupawakpa’s history is part of the wider story of Dakota communities in the northern Plains. A historical account published by Prairie History follows Dakota movement into what is now southwestern Manitoba and the establishment of the community also recorded as Oak Lake Sioux. The Nation’s Dakota identity and relationship with its lands should be distinguished from the histories of neighbouring numbered-treaty bands. The older name is useful when reading archival records, but does not describe a separate present-day Nation. Published accounts form only one part of this history, alongside the family knowledge and oral traditions held by the community.

Chemawawin Cree Nation describes a history deeply changed by the Grand Rapids hydroelectric project. Families had lived near the meeting of the Saskatchewan River and Cedar Lake, supported by the territory’s resources. Planning for the dam led to negotiations recorded in the 1962 Letter of Intent and the relocation of the community to another site on Cedar Lake. The Nation’s account describes major environmental, economic and social losses following that move. A November 9, 1990 settlement with Manitoba Hydro and later arrangements in 2004 and 2011 addressed aspects of the impacts. The Nation presents restoration as a continuing effort.

Cross Lake’s modern history includes the struggle over the effects of hydroelectric development on Pimicikamak lands and waters. In evidence to a parliamentary committee, community representatives described the Northern Flood Agreement and argued that its promises had not been fulfilled. Their testimony connected environmental changes with damage to livelihoods and community well-being. This record preserves the community’s position within a wider debate about hydro development and government responsibility. It is a selected account of a modern historical issue, rather than a complete history of Pimicikamak or a substitute for the knowledge held by its people.

Dakota Plains and Dakota Tipi share an administrative history connected with the Sioux Village settlement near Portage la Prairie. Dakota Tipi’s published account records the division of that settlement in 1972 into the two present-day First Nations. Dakota Plains is associated with lands adjoining Long Plain First Nation. This band separation was an administrative milestone within a longer Dakota history. The Sioux Village name connects older records with both communities.
connections: Dakota Plains and Dakota Tipi emerged as separate First Nations following the 1972 division of Sioux Village.

summary: Dakota Tipi First Nation’s own account records its creation as a separate First Nation in 1972, when the Sioux Village settlement near Portage la Prairie divided into Dakota Tipi and Dakota Plains. Dakota Tipi received reserve status that year on an initial land base of approximately 25 acres. The account describes later additions to those lands. These changes concern reserve administration and land holdings, rather than the beginning of the people’s Dakota history. The earlier Sioux Village name and the relationship with Dakota Plains are useful context when following the community through older government and settlement records.

Dauphin River First Nation experienced a major disruption when flooding in 2011 forced residents from their homes. Manitoba’s account of the community’s rebuilt school places it within Operation Return Home, the effort to restore communities affected by the floods. The school opened in 2018, providing a local place for students after years of displacement and recovery. This milestone illustrates the importance of rebuilding community institutions as well as houses and infrastructure. The flood and return-home process are part of Dauphin River’s recent history, rather than a full account of the Nation’s older relationship with its territory.

Ebb and Flow First Nation’s historical lands include a medicine wheel near Alonsa. A University of Winnipeg account describes how this place inspired artwork at the university, connecting the design with Indigenous history and knowledge. The installation carries elements of the medicine wheel’s pattern into a contemporary public setting. This is one documented example of the community’s historical relationship with places beyond the boundaries of its present settlement. The account provides a cultural and territorial milestone without treating the university artwork as the origin or full expression of the teachings connected with the original site.

Fisher River Cree Nation traces its community history to Cree families at Norway House whose livelihoods were affected by changes in the fur trade and transportation. Chief David Rundle and other representatives sought support for a move south in 1874. The Nation’s ancestors participated in Treaty 5 in 1875, and 43 families travelled to Fisher River in 1877 after a smallpox quarantine delayed the move. Families built homes, farmed and continued fishing, trapping and seasonal work. Additional families joined through the 1908 treaty adhesion. The Nation’s account emphasizes the continuing importance of language, traditions and fishing across generations.
connections: Fisher River’s history records the 1877 move of families from Norway House.

summary: Sagkeeng’s Anicinabe history is rooted in the Winnipeg River and Traverse Bay area. Its own account records ancestors’ participation in Treaty 1 in 1871 and the survey of Fort Alexander Indian Reserve in 1874. The older Fort Alexander name appears in many government and school records. The Nation’s timeline also documents the Fort Alexander residential school and the later development of community schools, including the Anicinabe Community School in 1975 and a new school in 2019. These events show changes in colonial administration and community institutions within a much longer history of Anicinabe life in the region.

Fox Lake Cree Nation’s history includes settlement around Fox Lake, Bird and Gillam along the Hudson Bay railway. Keewatin Tribal Council records federal recognition as a separate band in 1947, following separation from the York Factory First Nation. Its Treaty 5 relationship comes through the parent band’s 1910 adhesion. Bird became a reserve in 1985 and a home community was established there, while members also continued living in Gillam. These milestones explain the Nation’s connections to several communities and to York Factory. Band recognition and reserve creation describe administrative changes within a longer Cree history in northern Manitoba.
connections: Fox Lake became a separate band from York Factory in 1947.

summary: Gambler First Nation’s own history page connects the Nation’s name with Atakawinin Tanner, known as The Gambler. It identifies him as the grandson of John “Falcon” Tanner and the son of Chief Picheeto, or Edward Tanner. These family relationships provide a starting point for reading the community’s written history. The Nation also makes available The Silver Creek, a historical report that places the band within the treaty-era history of the region. These published materials preserve selected family and archival accounts; they do not replace the wider community knowledge carried by Gambler members.

Garden Hill’s history is linked with the earlier Island Lake band and its 1909 adhesion to Treaty 5. Four Arrows Regional Health Authority records that Garden Hill, Wasagamack, St. Theresa Point and Red Sucker Lake remained within a single band until 1969. The later division established separate First Nation administrations without erasing their shared regional history. Garden Hill is associated with the northern shore of Island Lake, and the source identifies the local language as the Island Lake Oji-Cree dialect. The treaty and band-division dates are selected administrative milestones within the much longer history of the Island Lake people.
connections: Garden Hill and Wasagamack belonged to the earlier Island Lake band until 1969.
Garden Hill and St. Theresa Point share the earlier Island Lake band history.
Garden Hill and Red Sucker Lake share the earlier Island Lake band history.

summary: God’s Lake First Nation’s treaty history includes the 1909 adhesion to Treaty 5, as recorded by Keewatin Tribal Council. God’s Lake Narrows is part of a wider northern Cree history associated with the lake and its waterways. A separate council account describes people moving from God’s Lake Narrows to God’s River in the mid-1940s; that community later became Manto Sipi Cree Nation. The source reports differing explanations for the move, so no single cause is assumed here. These treaty and community-formation milestones help distinguish the related Nations while recognizing their shared earlier administrative history.
connections: God’s River, now Manto Sipi, developed from the earlier God’s Lake community.

summary: Hollow Water First Nation’s published community account identifies Anishinabe as its Indigenous language and records a land-based economy that includes fishing, hunting, trapping and wild rice harvesting. These activities provide context for understanding the community’s relationship with its territory. The Nation also lists community institutions, ceremony grounds and the Wanipigow Producer Co-op. Its account emphasizes the preservation of cultural heritage alongside community well-being. This brief draws on that published description of cultural and economic continuity; it does not assign an unverified founding date, treaty-signing leader or origin story to the Nation.

summary: Keeseekoowenin Ojibway First Nation’s history is connected with Riding Mountain and the earlier Okanese band. Its account records Mekis succeeding Okanese and signing Treaty 2 in 1871. After Mekis died in 1874, his younger half-brother Keeseekoowenin, also known as Moses Burns, became Chief and served until 1906. The history describes community life through hunting, livestock, agriculture and travel routes in the Riding Mountain region. It also recognizes displacement associated with the creation of parks. These leadership and treaty milestones are part of a much longer Anishinabe relationship with the land, lakes and rivers.

Kinonjeoshtegon First Nation is a Chippewa community in Manitoba’s Interlake region, associated with the Jackhead reserves. The older Jackhead name appears in reserve records and remains useful when tracing the community through historical documents. Interlake Reserves Tribal Council identifies Jackhead 43 and 43A as the Nation’s reserve lands. Its published profile supplies community and institutional context, rather than a detailed chronology of treaty-era leaders or migration. This brief therefore preserves the documented identity and place names without assigning an unverified founding date. The Nation’s history extends beyond these reserve designations and administrative records.

Lake Manitoba First Nation is associated with Dog Creek Reserve 46 on the northeastern shore of the lake’s southern basin. A federal community profile records its participation in Treaty 2, signed in 1871, and identifies Ojibway as the community’s Indigenous language. The Dog Creek name is an important link between older reserve records and the present-day Nation. These records describe a treaty relationship and reserve geography rather than the beginning of the people’s history. They provide a starting point for understanding Lake Manitoba’s place within the Interlake region while leaving unverified leaders, migration dates and origin stories unspecified.
publisher: Indian and Northern Affairs Canada — 1997 community profiles

summary: Lake St. Martin First Nation experienced prolonged displacement following the 2011 Interlake flood. Research with Elders records the effects of evacuation on health, community life and the ability to practise land-based ways of living. The study places Elders’ understanding of minoaywin, or well-being, at the centre of recovery and healing. It shows that displacement concerns relationships with people and territory as well as the loss of houses. This account documents one major event in the Nation’s recent history and the knowledge shared by participants; it is not a complete account of Lake St. Martin’s older Indigenous history.
publisher: Canadian Journal on Aging — research with First Nations Elders

summary: Little Grand Rapids is an Anishinaabe community with ancestral lands on both sides of the Manitoba–Ontario boundary. Pimachiowin Aki’s community account describes longstanding canoe routes, family harvesting areas and the preservation of named places through Elders’ recorded knowledge. Community members are documenting Anishinaabemowin place names and their meanings so that this history remains available to future generations. The account also emphasizes that cultural places carry responsibilities and that some sacred areas should not be photographed. This history centres on living relationships with the land, language and waterways, rather than treating a reserve designation as the beginning of the community.

Little Saskatchewan First Nation was among the Interlake communities displaced by the 2011 flood. Research with Elders examines how forced displacement disrupted everyday relationships, cultural practices and well-being. Participants’ accounts stress the importance of community, land and traditional life in healing after evacuation. Their testimony helps document the human effects of flooding beyond damage to buildings and infrastructure. This is one part of Little Saskatchewan’s recent history, presented through the study’s community-based perspective. It does not establish a founding date or substitute for the Nation’s broader oral histories.
publisher: Canadian Journal on Aging — research with First Nations Elders

summary: Long Plain belongs to the Treaty 1 Nations, whose treaty relationship dates to 1871. A federal profile records the settlement of its outstanding treaty land entitlement on August 4, 1994. The Nation’s reserve lands are associated with the Assiniboine River near Portage la Prairie. These milestones connect treaty obligations with later efforts to secure land and support community development. They describe selected changes in administration and land holdings within a much longer Indigenous history.
publisher: Indian and Northern Affairs Canada — 2004 community profiles

summary: Manto Sipi Cree Nation’s history is connected with the earlier God’s Lake First Nation. Keewatin Tribal Council records that people moved from God’s Lake Narrows to establish the God’s River community in the mid-1940s. Its account notes different explanations for the separation, so the move is not assigned a single cause here. A ministerial order established God’s River First Nation on May 7, 1976. The Nation’s Treaty 5 relationship comes through the 1909 adhesion. These milestones distinguish the community’s formation and later band recognition from the longer Cree history of the lake and river region.

Marcel Colomb First Nation shares an earlier band history with Mathias Colomb. The Treaty Relations Commission of Manitoba records that a group of Mathias Colomb members voted in 1972 to establish a separate band and council. Official recognition of Marcel Colomb followed in 1995. This history links the Nation with Treaty 6 through its earlier community relationship. The years of the vote and recognition describe a process of administrative separation; they do not mark the beginning of Cree identity or of families’ relationships with northern Manitoba. The two present-day Nations each maintain their own community and governance.
connections: Marcel Colomb’s separate-band process began with a 1972 vote by members of Mathias Colomb.

summary: Mathias Colomb Cree Nation’s own timeline describes a history rooted in the Churchill River region. In 1910, following separation from the Peter Ballantyne band at Pelican Narrows, the community settled along the river at Highrock Lake. The account identifies Mathias Colomb as the first Chief, serving until his death in 1932. Prayer River was surveyed as a reserve under the band on August 29, 1926. A later fire destroyed that community and its residents moved to Pukatawagan. These selected milestones describe changes in settlement and band administration within a much longer history of Cree life in the boreal north.

Minegoziibe Anishinabe’s published community account traces its Saulteaux ancestors to the Lake Superior and Sault Ste. Marie region. Families made their home along the southwestern shore of Lake Winnipegosis, where fish, waterfowl and wild game supported community life. The account identifies the people as Plains Ojibwe or Anishinaabe and explains the French-derived Saulteaux name through its association with rapids. Pine Creek is another name encountered in records of the Nation. These accounts describe ancestry, movement and land-based life, rather than treating the establishment of a reserve as the beginning of Indigenous history.
publisher: Government of Anishinaabe Nation in Treaty 2 Territory

summary: Misipawistik Cree Nation’s history is closely connected with the Saskatchewan River rapids at Grand Rapids. The Lake Winnipeg Indigenous Collective describes how hydroelectric construction and the rerouting of the river in the 1960s left a dry riverbed where the rapids had been. This transformation changed an important feature of the community’s territory and its relationship with the water. The Collective’s Misipawistik perspectives project records community experience of these changes. The hydroelectric period is therefore a major part of the Nation’s recent history, while Cree relationships with the river and surrounding lands extend beyond the dam’s construction.

Mosakahiken Cree Nation’s treaty history is recorded under Treaty 5. The federal treaty table lists its adhesion date as September 7, 1876. The Nation is also known through the Moose Lake place name, which appears in historical and community records. Its Treaty 5 relationship should be distinguished from later band administration and from the much longer Cree history of the region. These published records provide a confirmed treaty milestone, but do not establish an origin date for the people. No historical Chief or migration story is assigned here without a source connecting that detail specifically to Mosakahiken.
publisher: Indian and Northern Affairs Canada — Basic Departmental Data 2003

summary: Nisichawayasihk Cree Nation locates its history where the Burntwood, Footprint and Rat rivers meet. Its own historical account emphasizes Nehetho language, storytelling and responsibilities to the ancestral homeland. Chief Pierre Moose and councillors Murdoch Hart and James Spence represented the community at the Treaty 5 adhesion ceremony at Nelson House on July 30, 1908. The Nation explains that its ancestors sought to safeguard their way of life and understood treaty-making through sharing and continuing relationships with the land. The treaty and reserve milestones belong within this much longer history, rather than defining its beginning.

Northlands Denesuline’s community overview links its history with the earlier Barren Lands band at Brochet. The timeline records the Treaty 10 adhesion at Brochet on August 19, 1907, with Chief Petit Casimir among the signatories. Families began moving from Brochet to Lac Brochet in September 1973, building log homes at the new settlement. On March 21, 1978, Lac Brochet residents voted to divide the Barren Lands band and create Northlands. These events explain the relationship between the two present-day Nations. The band division was an administrative milestone within a much longer Denesuline history in the region.
connections: Northlands was created through division of the earlier Barren Lands band.
publisher: Northlands Denesuline / Teach For Canada — community overview

summary: Norway House Cree Nation’s history page places the community within the inland fur-trade transportation network. A post was built at Mossy Point in 1817, and the later post site was established in 1825–26. Norway House became an important Hudson’s Bay Company depot and meeting place. The Nation records the signing of Treaty 5 there on September 24, 1875. Its account also notes the development of Cree syllabics associated with James Evans and the designation of Norway House as a national historic site in 1932. These written milestones form part of the wider Cree history of the area.

O-Chi-Chak-Ko-Sipi First Nation is associated with Crane River Reserve 51 on the northern basin of Lake Manitoba. A federal historical profile records its Treaty 2 relationship, dating to 1871, and identifies Ojibway as the community’s Indigenous language. The Crane River name provides a link between older reserve records and the present-day Nation. Reserve geography and treaty participation are documented milestones within a longer Anishinaabe history. The nearby non-reserve community has its own municipal history, so its incorporation dates should not be treated as the founding dates of the First Nation.
publisher: Indian and Northern Affairs Canada — 1994 community profiles

summary: O-Pipon-Na-Piwin Cree Nation’s history includes community efforts to restore land-based food knowledge at South Indian Lake. A research account describes how Elders and local food champions organized harvesting activities and training for young people. In 2012 they developed Ithinto Mechisowin, a year-round program whose name refers to food from the land. The program connects food, health, heritage and the renewal of community knowledge. A Treaty Relations Commission report also records a July 2010 commemoration of the Nation’s July 2006 Treaty 5 adhesion. Together these accounts document treaty recognition and community-led cultural continuity.

summary: Opaskwayak Cree Nation’s educational authority describes a sustained movement toward community control of schooling. A 1979 study examined why students faced difficulty in the provincial system, identifying marginalization and cultural and language differences. Community consultation supported building a school and educating children on reserve. An alternative school opened in 1984 while negotiations continued for a kindergarten-to-Grade-12 school. This history records the work of families, educators and leadership to shape education around the needs of their children. It is one part of Opaskwayak’s broader history, told through the Nation’s own educational institution.

Pauingassi’s community history connects its name with nearby sand hills and recalls the area as a place for gathering and ceremony. Pimachiowin Aki records that Pauingassi and Little Grand Rapids were recognized within one band following the 1876 Treaty 5 adhesion. Pauingassi received reserve status in 1988 and became a separate First Nation in 1991, near the original village at Fishing Lake. The account also remembers Naamiwan, or Fair Wind, an Anishinaabe healer and leader. These milestones bring together cultural history and later administrative changes without reducing the community’s origins to the date of band recognition.
connections: Pauingassi and Little Grand Rapids were administered as one band before Pauingassi became separate in 1991.

summary: Peguis First Nation is named for Chief Peguis, who led Saulteaux people from the Sault Ste. Marie region to Manitoba in the late eighteenth century. Treaty One’s community account identifies both Ojibway and Cree ancestry among its members. The Nation belongs to the Treaty 1 relationship, originating in the agreement signed at Lower Fort Garry on August 3, 1871. The history of Chief Peguis and the later treaty relationship represent different periods and should not be collapsed into a claim that he signed that treaty. These selected milestones provide context for the Nation’s name, ancestry and place in Manitoba’s history.

facts.Ancestral movement: Sault Ste. Marie to Manitoba, late 1700s

summary: Pinaymootang’s published community account connects Fairford with the earlier Partridge Crop place name. The area appears in fur-trade records through Duncan Cameron’s winter there in 1795–96 and John Richards McKay’s posting in 1846. A mission, store and church were established during the nineteenth century, and the Hudson’s Bay Company operated Fairford Post from 1871 until 1913. These are milestones in the written history of trade and colonial institutions at the settlement. They provide context for the Nation’s territory without treating the arrival of traders or missionaries as the beginning of Indigenous life there.
publisher: Government of Anishinaabe Nation in Treaty 2 Territory

summary: Poplar River First Nation’s community account describes archaeological evidence of at least 7,000 years of continuous occupation in the area. Its leaders signed Treaty 5 on September 20, 1875. The Nation’s traditional territory extends east from Lake Winnipeg toward Ontario and is known as Asatiwisipe Aki. A community-based lands management plan became law in 2011, with the traditional lands designated a protected area. In 2018, the territories of Poplar River and three partner Nations became part of the Pimachiowin Aki World Heritage Site. The account links these milestones with continuing harvesting, fishing and family responsibilities to the land.

Red Sucker Lake’s treaty history includes the 1909 adhesion to Treaty 5. Four Arrows Regional Health Authority identifies the community’s language as the Island Lake Oji-Cree dialect. The regional history also links Red Sucker Lake with Garden Hill, Wasagamack and St. Theresa Point through the earlier Island Lake band, which divided in 1969. These connections explain a shared administrative past while recognizing distinct present-day Nations. The treaty and band-division dates describe selected milestones, rather than the beginning of Anisininew history or of families’ relationships with the lakes and lands of the region.

summary: Rolling River First Nation’s history includes an enduring relationship with the Riding Mountain region. Parks Canada records Rolling River among the seven Nations participating in the Coalition of First Nations with Interests in Riding Mountain National Park. A ministerial agreement in 2006 established a forum for these Nations and Parks Canada to work together. The coalition addresses historical relationships with the area and supports the presentation of First Nation history and culture in the park. This is a documented modern institutional milestone within a much older relationship with the land, rather than a founding date for Rolling River.

summary: Roseau River Anishinaabe First Nation’s account through Treaty One locates its history in the Red River and Pembina valleys. It identifies the community with the Strong Heart People and with the Treaty 1 relationship established in 1871. The Nation’s later history includes a land-claim settlement in 2011 and the creation of a trust connected with that settlement. These milestones bring together cultural identity, treaty obligations and efforts to address historical land issues. They describe selected parts of Roseau River’s published history, while the community’s relationship with its territory and its oral traditions extend beyond the treaty and settlement dates.

Sandy Bay Ojibway First Nation’s own account recalls the earlier White Mud band name and its distinction from the Portage band led by Chief Yellow Quill. It connects the community’s later settlement with the Treaty 1 era and records Nawachegapow as an early post-treaty Chief. The Nation’s lands are on the western shore of Lake Manitoba. Its account emphasizes the importance of keeping Ojibway language alive across generations. Some dates on the page are inconsistent, so this brief retains the documented names and broad treaty-era context without assigning a disputed exact date to the community’s establishment.

Sapotaweyak Cree Nation’s history appears in older records under the Shoal River name. A federal community profile records its Treaty 4 relationship, dating to 1874, and identifies Cree as the community’s Indigenous language. The Nation’s settlement is associated with Dawson Bay and the northern Lake Winnipegosis region, beside Pelican Rapids. Its reserve records retain the Shoal River name, linking historical documents with the present-day Nation. These published details provide a treaty and territorial framework for the brief; they do not establish the beginning of Cree life in the region or supply an unverified treaty-signing Chief.

summary: Sayisi Dene history includes the forced relocation from the Little Duck Lake region to Churchill in 1956. Canada’s later apology acknowledged that the decision caused profound harm to the community and disrupted a way of life connected with the land and caribou. Families subsequently worked to return to a land-based community at Tadoule Lake in 1973. The federal government delivered its formal apology on August 16, 2016. These events are central to the community’s recent history of displacement, return and rebuilding. They form part of a much longer Sayisi Dene relationship with northern lands and waters.

summary: Shamattawa First Nation’s treaty history includes an adhesion to Treaty 5 on August 10, 1910, as recorded in federal departmental data. This was later than the treaty’s original negotiations in the 1870s and should be described as an adhesion rather than an original 1875 signing. Keewatin Tribal Council places the community at the meeting of the Gods and Echoing rivers in northern Manitoba. These records provide a confirmed treaty milestone and geographical context. They do not establish a founding date for the community or justify assigning a historical Chief without a source connecting that person to Shamattawa.

summary: Sioux Valley Dakota Nation’s recent history includes a long effort to secure self-government. The Nation’s own account records the implementation of its self-government arrangements on July 1, 2014, following years of negotiations with Canada and Manitoba. The agreements created a framework for government-to-government relationships and for the Nation to exercise authority in community affairs. Sioux Valley identifies as Wipazoka Wakpa Oyate and grounds its government in Dakota identity and traditions. The 2014 milestone concerns the recognition and operation of modern governance arrangements; it does not mark the beginning of the people’s own laws or history.

Skownan First Nation appears in older records as the Waterhen River Band of Saulteaux and later Waterhen First Nation. Its published community account identifies a Treaty 2 relationship and connects the Skownan name with an Anishinaabe expression referring to turning around a point. The community is associated with Waterhen Reserve 45 and the Waterhen Lake region. The older Waterhen name can cause confusion with Waterhen Lake First Nation in Saskatchewan, a separate Cree Nation. These names and treaty details help readers follow Skownan through historical records while recognizing its distinct Saulteaux identity and longer relationship with the land.

summary: St. Theresa Point’s treaty history includes the 1909 adhesion to Treaty 5. Four Arrows Regional Health Authority identifies the local language as the Island Lake Oji-Cree dialect and places the community on the southwestern shore of Island Lake. The regional account links it with the earlier Island Lake band alongside Garden Hill, Wasagamack and Red Sucker Lake, until the division in 1969. These milestones explain the shared administrative history of the four present-day Nations. They form one part of the longer history of the Island Lake people and their relationships with the region’s lands and waters.

summary: Swan Lake First Nation is an Anishinabe community whose published account identifies Saulteaux as its Indigenous language. It belongs to the Treaty 1 relationship established in 1871. Treaty One’s community profile describes a land base distributed among the main Swan Lake reserve, Carberry, Indian Gardens and Headingley. A treaty land entitlement settlement enabled the Nation to expand its lands for future community and economic development. This later land history is part of the continuing implementation of treaty obligations. It should be distinguished from the much older history of the people and from the dates of individual reserve additions.

summary: Tataskweyak Cree Nation’s own environmental evaluation places its history within a continuing relationship with the homeland around Split Lake. The report records the 1908 adhesion to Treaty 5 and the earlier official names Split Lake Indian Band and Split Lake Cree Nation. It explains that ancestors approached treaty discussions through an understanding of sharing land and resources while continuing their way of life. The report also describes the profound changes in authority that followed colonial administration. This community-authored account provides a perspective on treaty history, rather than treating a government reserve designation as the beginning of Tataskweyak identity.

publisher: Cree Nation Partners — Keeyask Environmental Evaluation, 2012

summary: Tootinaowaziibeeng Treaty Reserve’s published community account identifies it as an Anishinabe Nation associated with Valley River Reserve 63A east of Roblin. The account places its history within a wider network of Ojibway communities around the Duck Mountain and Riding Mountain regions. It describes relationships with the earlier Swan River communities and other neighbouring Nations. This regional perspective helps explain why community histories extend beyond present reserve boundaries. The account is retained as the publishing organization’s description of those relationships; it is not used to assign a different numbered treaty or an unverified exact date to the Nation’s origins.
publisher: Government of Anishinaabe Nation in Treaty 2 Territory

summary: War Lake First Nation is associated with Ilford in northern Manitoba. Keewatin Tribal Council’s account describes Ilford’s development as a construction and service centre during the building of the Hudson Bay Railway. It later served as a marshalling point for prospectors during the Island Lake gold rush and for winter freight roads extending eastward. These milestones concern the written history of the settlement and transportation network. They should not be treated as the origin of Cree life in the area. The Nation’s own history and families’ relationships with the region extend beyond the railway-era description.

Wasagamack’s history includes the 1909 adhesion to Treaty 5 and the later division of the Island Lake band. Four Arrows Regional Health Authority records that Wasagamack, Garden Hill, St. Theresa Point and Red Sucker Lake remained part of one band until 1969. Wasagamack’s community is on the western shore of Island Lake, and its language is identified as the Island Lake Oji-Cree dialect. The shared band history explains relationships among the four Nations while preserving their distinct present-day identities. These treaty and administrative milestones are selected events within the longer history of the Island Lake people.

Waywayseecappo First Nation’s traditional knowledge study, See What the Land Gave Us, documents relationships with lands and resources across generations. Prepared in 2017, the study draws on community interviews and earlier knowledge recorded in 1982. It connects historical land use with accounts of changes experienced over the following decades. The report identifies Waywayseecappo as an Ojibway community and a Treaty 4 Nation. This community-based record preserves a perspective that extends beyond reserve boundaries and administrative dates. It offers a starting point for understanding the Nation’s history through the experiences and knowledge of its own members.

summary: Wuskwi Sipihk First Nation appears in earlier records as Indian Birch. A federal community profile records its earlier connection with Sapotaweyak, or Shoal River, and its establishment as a separate reserve in September 1982. The profile identifies Cree as the Indigenous language and Treaty 4, signed in 1874, as the treaty relationship. Swan Lake Reserve 65C is associated with the Nation, distinct from the Swan Lake First Nation in southern Manitoba. These names and dates help distinguish the communities in archival records and explain Wuskwi Sipihk’s shared earlier administrative history with Sapotaweyak.

summary: York Factory First Nation’s published history connects the people of York Landing with the Hayes River and the former Hudson’s Bay Company post at York Factory near Hudson Bay. Keewatin Tribal Council records that closure of the company’s store in 1957 was a major factor in the relocation to York Landing that year. The new community received reserve status in 1989. These changes linked fur-trade history with displacement and the establishment of a different settlement on the Nelson River. The relocation and reserve dates describe selected modern milestones within the people’s much longer Cree history in northern Manitoba.
